paragraphs: This paper investigates why tokenization can make a major difference to language modeling, using controlled sequence generators rather than natural language. The generators are higher-order Markov processes, where the next character depends on several preceding characters. For certain such processes, the authors observe that transformers trained directly on characters learn extremely slowly or fail to capture these dependencies.

In these experiments, unsuccessful character-level models behave like unigram predictors: they predict individual characters without adequately using the surrounding sequence. Introducing tokenization changes the outcome. The transformers can then assign probabilities to sequences close to those of the generating process, achieving low cross-entropy loss.

The theoretical analysis explains how an appropriate tokenization can make even a simple unigram model over tokens nearly optimal for these Markov sources. Grouping characters into tokens can therefore change what a simple predictor is able to represent effectively. The result supplies a justification for tokenization within the studied setting; it does not establish that every transformer or every language-modeling problem requires tokenization.
neurips-2024-an-analysis-of-tokenization.tldr: On certain Markov-generated sequences, appropriate tokenization lets even simple token predictors model dependencies that character-level transformers struggle to learn.

paragraphs: Statistical analysis requires more than recognizing the name of a procedure: a model must also determine whether that procedure applies to the problem. This paper introduces StatQA to evaluate both specialized statistical tasks and judgments about method applicability, with particular attention to hypothesis testing. The benchmark contains 11,623 examples.

The authors test representative language models with several prompting strategies. GPT-4o reaches a best reported performance of 64.83%, showing substantial remaining difficulty on the benchmark. Open-source models such as LLaMA-3 initially show limited capability, but fine-tuned models improve markedly and outperform all the evaluated approaches that rely on examples supplied in context.

Comparisons with human participants reveal a difference in the kinds of mistakes made. Models mainly choose methods where they do not apply, while humans more often confuse the statistical task itself. These findings distinguish procedural knowledge from knowing when to use it. They also motivate investigating human–model collaboration, although complementary error patterns alone do not demonstrate that such collaboration will improve results.
neurips-2024-are-large-language-models-g.tldr: StatQA finds substantial weaknesses in language models’ statistical judgments, especially deciding when a method applies, while fine-tuning improves performance.

paragraphs: Vision-language models encode images and text into representations used for tasks such as classification, retrieval, and image generation. These representations can carry societal biases from training data, including negative associations involving racial or gender identities. BendVLM addresses how to adjust such representations when a model is being used.

The paper identifies drawbacks in two existing approaches. Fine-tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting, where modifying a model damages previously learned capabilities. Methods that avoid fine-tuning commonly assume that unwanted correlations can be described by one linear direction shared across all inputs. That assumption limits how flexibly the correction can respond to different examples.

BendVLM instead proposes a nonlinear correction tailored to each individual input, without fine-tuning the underlying model. It also does not require the complete set of future inputs to be known before inference. This makes its design suited to online settings, including retrieval and text-guided image generation, where requests arrive over time. The contribution is a more input-sensitive debiasing approach, rather than a claim that all societal bias is eliminated.
neurips-2024-bendvlm-test-time-debiasing.tldr: BendVLM proposes input-specific, nonlinear debiasing of vision-language embeddings at inference time without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: TransCLIP improves vision-language predictions by using the structure of an unlabeled collection of examples. This approach, called transduction, lets information across the collection influence predictions. The method can be added to existing zero-shot and few-shot models, extending models that otherwise make predictions through their previously learned rules.

Its objective combines fitting the unlabeled data with a constraint that preserves guidance from the text encoder. The constraint uses KL divergence to keep the transductive process informed by language knowledge. This matters because a method relying only on visual features would leave out the textual information that helps define a vision-language model’s predictions.

The authors derive an iterative optimization procedure with guaranteed convergence and separate updates for sample assignments, supporting computationally efficient use on large datasets. Their evaluations report consistent improvements to the tested zero-shot and few-shot models. TransCLIP also substantially outperforms evaluated transductive methods based only on vision features, with the language constraint identified as an important contributor. The findings support using unlabeled data and text guidance together.
neurips-2024-boosting-vision-language-mo.tldr: TransCLIP improves tested vision-language models by combining unlabeled-data structure with a constraint that preserves text-encoder guidance.

paragraphs: DistillNeRF learns to represent outdoor driving scenes in 3D from a sparse set of camera images captured at a single moment. The camera views have limited overlap, making geometry difficult to infer. Its feedforward model predicts a scene representation and learns through differentiable rendering that reconstructs color, depth, or feature images.

The method combines two sources of supervision. Neural Radiance Fields optimized for individual scenes supply dense depth information and targets from virtual cameras, helping teach geometry beyond what the sparse input views directly reveal. Features from pretrained image models such as CLIP and DINOv2 supply semantic information without costly human annotations of 3D scenes. A two-stage encoder and sparse hierarchical voxel representation bring these sources together.

On NuScenes and Waymo NOTR, the authors report substantial improvements over comparable self-supervised methods in reconstruction, novel-view synthesis, and depth estimation. The representation also supports competitive zero-shot semantic occupancy prediction and open-world scene understanding. These results connect geometric reconstruction with semantic understanding within one learned 3D representation.
neurips-2024-distillnerf-perceiving-3d-s.tldr: DistillNeRF transfers geometry from scene-specific neural fields and semantics from image foundation models to infer rich 3D scenes from sparse camera views.

paragraphs: A reward function can direct an AI system toward behavior that differs from what its user intended. This paper argues that understanding such misspecification requires examining the user’s beliefs about the agent. It introduces Expectation Alignment, a formal framework that uses those beliefs to explain what it means for an objective to be misspecified and for the mismatch to be resolved.

The framework treats expectations about system behavior as part of the problem, rather than interpreting the supplied reward in isolation. The authors use this perspective to explain existing approaches, identify limitations in how they handle reward misspecification, and derive possible new strategies for addressing it.

They then propose an interactive algorithm that works backward from the specified reward to infer potential user expectations. The inference can be expressed as linear programs, providing an efficient implementation route. The method is evaluated on standard Markov Decision Process benchmarks. The contribution joins a formal account of expectation mismatch with a concrete algorithm for investigating and addressing it.
neurips-2024-expectation-alignment-handl.tldr: Expectation Alignment formalizes reward misspecification through users’ beliefs about an agent and derives an interactive method for inferring their expectations.

paragraphs: Models that combine several kinds of input can learn unevenly across those inputs. One modality may fit category labels more readily than another, causing their component models to converge at different rates. This paper treats that difference in label-fitting difficulty as a central cause of modality imbalance and the optimization problems that follow.

The proposed method combines supervised multimodal training with unsupervised contrastive learning. Contrastive learning acts as an additional training signal that can intervene in how each modality learns to fit category labels. The balance between these objectives changes during training, allowing the method to respond to differences in learning progress.

The authors first show that a simple heuristic for combining the objectives can significantly reduce modality imbalance. They then introduce a learned integration strategy that adjusts the two losses dynamically and further improves performance. Experiments on widely used datasets report better results than the compared state-of-the-art multimodal methods. The findings suggest that balancing modalities can benefit from changing their learning signals, alongside adjusting the training procedure.
neurips-2024-facilitating-multimodal-cla.tldr: Dynamically combining contrastive and supervised learning reduces modality imbalance and improves classification in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning methods for Boolean satisfiability need training problems that resemble practical workloads and remain challenging to solve. Available datasets often provide random instances or only a few examples from unrelated families. HardCore Generation addresses this shortage by generating difficult unsatisfiable problems from existing examples, with attention to both realism and generation cost.

The method focuses on cores, the parts of a problem identified as key contributors to its difficulty. Detecting these with traditional heuristic procedures can be expensive, undermining the scalability of generation. The authors introduce a graph neural network for fast core detection, then use core identification and manipulation as the basis for creating additional problems.

Empirical results show that the generated instances remain hard to solve while retaining important attributes of the original examples. The authors also use them to augment training data for predicting solver runtimes and observe improved predictions. This establishes a concrete use for the synthetic data: helping models estimate problem-solving cost, beyond merely producing more satisfiability instances.
neurips-2024-hardcore-generation-generat.tldr: HardCore Generation uses graph-based core detection to efficiently create difficult unsatisfiable problems that improve solver-runtime prediction through data augmentation.

paragraphs: A model with access to fewer features can still be highly accurate within that restricted setting. This paper asks how such a model can help train a richer model that sees more information. The restricted model can come from auxiliary data or from deliberately limiting the features available in the same dataset.

Induced Model Matching aligns the full model’s context-restricted behavior with the restricted model. The key is to compare models under matching information constraints, taking the nature of the restriction seriously. The authors relate this principle to noising and reverse knowledge distillation, showing that those approaches can be understood as approximations and can have consistency problems.

Experiments begin with logistic regression and extend to language modeling, where bigram models help train both LSTM and transformer models. A further reinforcement-learning example shows that policies based on partial observations can help learn better policies for fully observed problems. Together, these examples illustrate how restricted models can provide useful training information when restricted data is cheaper or the simpler learning problem is easier.
neurips-2024-induced-model-matching-rest.tldr: Induced Model Matching uses accurate restricted-feature models to guide richer models by aligning their behavior under the same information restriction.

paragraphs: Accepting a long input does not ensure that a language model uses information throughout it. This paper addresses the lost-in-the-middle problem and hypothesizes that long-context training provides too little explicit supervision showing that crucial information can appear anywhere. Its proposed response is information-intensive training, called IN2.

IN2 uses synthetic question-answer examples with contexts ranging from 4K to 32K tokens. Answering requires attending closely to short segments of about 128 tokens, as well as combining and reasoning across two or more segments. Applied to Mistral-7B, this training produces FILM-7B. The data therefore exercises both locating small pieces of information and using several pieces together.

The authors evaluate document, code, and structured-data contexts with several retrieval patterns. FILM-7B robustly retrieves information from different positions within its 32K window in these probes. It also improves on real-world long-context tasks: NarrativeQA F1 rises from 23.5 to 26.9, while MMLU accuracy remains comparable at 59.3 versus 59.2. These findings support the training approach without establishing the hypothesized cause as definitive.
neurips-2024-make-your-llm-fully-utilize.tldr: IN2 trains models to locate and combine information throughout long inputs, improving FILM-7B’s long-context performance while preserving comparable short-context results.

paragraphs: MAN TruckScenes provides a research dataset for studying how autonomous trucks perceive their surroundings. Truck-specific conditions include views blocked by trailers, different sensor perspectives, and terminal environments. The dataset brings these challenges into more than 740 recordings, each lasting 20 seconds, across varied environmental conditions.

The sensor setup combines four cameras, six lidar sensors, six radar sensors, two inertial measurement units, and high-precision satellite positioning. Its manually annotated and reviewed 3D bounding boxes cover 27 object classes, 15 attributes, and distances beyond 230 meters. Objects are tracked through each recording, while 34 scene tags describe the situations represented.

The paper also presents dataset analysis and baseline results, giving researchers a starting point for developing and comparing perception methods. The authors identify it as the first autonomous-trucking multimodal dataset and the first dataset with full-surround 4D radar coverage, as well as the largest radar dataset with annotated 3D boxes. Its contribution is a truck-focused evaluation and training resource for perception research relevant to road safety.
neurips-2024-man-truckscenes-a-multimoda.tldr: MAN TruckScenes supplies annotated, multimodal truck recordings that expose truck-specific perception challenges across diverse conditions.

paragraphs: This paper develops a view of learning inspired by natural systems that process environmental information as it arrives. Its central concern is spatiotemporal locality: representation and learning should interact through processes that are local in space and time. The authors seek a mathematical foundation for such learning before choosing a particular algorithm.

Drawing on ideas from theoretical physics, they derive learning laws with the structure of Hamiltonian equations. An algorithmic interpretation of these laws yields a local propagation procedure. A key theoretical connection is that the procedure reduces to backpropagation in the limit where information propagates infinitely fast.

That limiting relationship connects the proposed dynamics to an established training method while making propagation speed part of the formulation. The paper presents this as a route toward fully online learning based on local information processing. Its contribution is the derivation and conceptual connection: it opens a research direction in which the proposed local algorithm could replace backpropagation, rather than reporting a broad empirical demonstration of superior performance.
neurips-2024-nature-inspired-local-propa.tldr: The paper derives local learning dynamics that reduce to backpropagation when propagation speed tends to infinity.

paragraphs: This paper studies autoregressive decision trees as an architecture for language modeling. These trees were originally proposed for time-series problems, but the authors examine both what they can compute through sequential generation and what they can learn in language tasks. The work combines theoretical expressiveness results with practical experiments.

The analysis shows that intermediate chain-of-thought computations allow these models to simulate automata, Turing machines, and sparse circuits. It also bounds the tree size, depth, and computational resources involved. These results explain how sequential computation can give decision-tree models substantial expressive power, even though their building blocks differ from those of transformers.

In experiments on simple language-generation tasks, trained trees produce coherent, grammatically correct text at a level comparable to a smaller transformer. The authors also show that trees placed on top of transformer representations can solve complex reasoning tasks. The empirical comparison is specific to the reported tasks, while the broader contribution is to establish autoregressive trees as a computationally capable alternative worth exploring in language-model architecture.
neurips-2024-on-the-power-of-decision-tr.tldr: Autoregressive decision trees show strong theoretical computational abilities and promising results on simple text generation and reasoning over transformer representations.

paragraphs: OSLO studies whether an attacker can identify examples that belonged to a model’s training set when the model returns only a predicted class label. The proposed membership-inference attack uses a single target-model query per sample. This is a substantial reduction from the roughly 6,000 queries used by the compared state-of-the-art label-only attacks.

The method uses transfer-based adversarial perturbations. Its central idea is that training examples tend to resist these perturbations more than examples outside the training set. That difference provides a membership signal even when prediction probabilities are unavailable. The single-query claim concerns access to the target model, whose response is only a hard label.

The reported comparisons show higher precision and higher true-positive rates at matched false-positive rates. For a ResNet18 model on CIFAR100, OSLO achieves at least seven times the true-positive rate at a 1% false-positive rate and at least 22 times at 0.1%. The authors also evaluate several defenses. The findings demonstrate that restricting model outputs to labels can still leave substantial training-membership information exposed.
neurips-2024-oslo-one-shot-label-only-me.tldr: OSLO infers training-set membership with one label-only target query and outperforms the compared attacks in reported privacy evaluations.

paragraphs: In partially observed reinforcement learning, an agent often summarizes its observation history using stacked frames or a recurrent network. Such an agent state can be updated without knowing the environment model. However, it need not preserve the Markov property: the summary may omit history relevant to predicting what happens next.

Standard Q-learning learns a stationary policy, meaning that its decision rule for an agent state stays the same over time. The authors use examples to show that, when the state summary lacks the Markov property, allowing the decision rule to vary with time can improve performance. They propose PASQL, a Q-learning variant that learns policies whose decision rules repeat periodically.

Using periodic Markov chains and stochastic approximation, the paper proves convergence to a cyclic limit and characterizes the resulting policy’s approximation error. A numerical experiment demonstrates benefits of periodic policies over stationary ones. The central insight is that a repeating schedule of decision rules can be useful when an agent’s internal state is an imperfect summary of its history.
neurips-2024-periodic-agent-state-based-.tldr: PASQL learns periodic policies that can outperform stationary policies when an agent’s history summary does not satisfy the Markov property.

paragraphs: Diffusion transformers can generate high-quality images, but inference requires substantial computation. PTQ4DiT targets this cost through post-training quantization, which represents weights and activations with fewer bits. The paper identifies two obstacles specific to these models: some channels contain extremely large values, and prominent activation patterns change across diffusion timesteps.

Channel-wise Salience Balancing redistributes extreme magnitudes by exploiting complementary channel magnitudes, reducing quantization error in both weights and activations. A second component, Spearman’s rho-guided Salience Calibration, accounts for how activation salience changes over time. Together, these components address both uneven values across channels and variation during the generation process.

The authors also introduce offline reparameterization so that the method’s adjustments do not add computation during inference. Experiments show that eight-bit weights and eight-bit activations preserve comparable generation ability. The method also enables effective four-bit weight quantization while retaining eight-bit activations. These findings demonstrate that accommodating channel extremes and temporal variation can make low-precision diffusion transformers more practical.
neurips-2024-ptq4dit-post-training-quant.tldr: PTQ4DiT handles extreme channel values and changing activations to quantize diffusion transformers while preserving comparable generation ability at eight-bit precision.

paragraphs: Reward models learn from human preferences and guide language models during reinforcement learning from human feedback. When they generalize poorly to unfamiliar prompts or responses, optimizing their scores too aggressively can reduce actual performance. This paper addresses that reward over-optimization problem by improving the reward model’s internal representations.

The method retains the base model’s language-generation head while training a reward head on the same hidden states. Additional text-generation losses encourage those shared representations to preserve their ability to support language generation. Reward learning therefore takes place alongside an objective that maintains useful generative capabilities in the underlying representation.

The authors report markedly better reward-model accuracy across several out-of-distribution tasks and reduced over-optimization during reinforcement learning. This approach targets the quality of the learned reward signal, complementing the concern that policy optimization itself may need constraints. The results support hidden-state regularization as a way to make preference learning more robust when prompts and responses differ from those seen in reward-model training.
neurips-2024-regularizing-hidden-states-.tldr: Preserving text-generation capabilities while training a reward model improves its reported generalization and reduces reward over-optimization.

paragraphs: Layout-to-image generation creates pictures from predefined arrangements of objects. When those objects have detailed textual descriptions, the model must represent both the requested placement and the rich content associated with each region. This paper introduces a regional cross-attention module intended to improve that regional representation.

The authors report that the module is particularly helpful for complex descriptions that existing methods struggle to handle. Its purpose is to strengthen how the generation process represents individual layout regions. This connects the method directly to a demanding part of the task: translating detailed descriptions into appropriately represented parts of an image.

The paper also identifies a mismatch between training and evaluation. Open-vocabulary systems are trained in an open-set setting but often tested in closed-set environments. The authors propose two metrics for assessing open-vocabulary layout-to-image generation and conduct a comprehensive user study to validate their consistency with human preferences. The work thus addresses both generation quality and whether evaluation reflects the broader conditions these systems are designed to handle.
neurips-2024-rethinking-the-training-and.tldr: The paper improves regional modeling for detailed layout-to-image generation and introduces open-vocabulary evaluation metrics checked against human preferences.

paragraphs: Language-model applications often involve several generation calls connected by branching logic, parallel work, and structured inputs or outputs. SGLang is a system for programming and executing these more complex workflows efficiently. It combines a frontend language for describing the application with a runtime responsible for carrying out the work.

The frontend supplies primitives for generation and control of parallel execution. The runtime includes RadixAttention, which enables reuse of the key-value cache used during model inference. It also uses compressed finite-state machines to accelerate decoding when outputs must follow a prescribed structure. These optimizations target recurring work and constraints within language-model programs.

Experiments cover language and multimodal models across agent control, reasoning, few-shot tasks, JSON generation, retrieval-augmented pipelines, and multi-turn conversation. SGLang achieves up to 6.4 times the throughput of the compared state-of-the-art inference systems. That figure is the maximum reported improvement across the evaluated settings. The contribution is an integrated programming and execution system that makes complex model workflows more efficient.
neurips-2024-sglang-efficient-execution-.tldr: SGLang combines a programming frontend with optimized execution, achieving up to 6.4 times higher throughput in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Recovering several sharp frames from one blurred image is difficult because the image contains limited information about motion over time. Spike cameras provide an additional motion signal through sampling rates of up to 40,000 Hz. SpikeReveal uses these streams to guide reconstruction while addressing the poor real-world transfer of supervised methods trained on synthetic data.

The authors first formulate relationships among spike streams, blurred images, and the underlying sharp sequence. They then build a self-supervised cascade to handle spike noise and mismatched spatial resolution, two obstacles to using that formulation directly. This connects the reconstruction process to both the image and the accompanying temporal measurements.

Knowledge distillation and a re-blurring loss are used to develop a lightweight deblurring network that produces sequences consistent with the input’s brightness and texture. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on real and synthetic datasets support improved generalization. The contribution is a self-supervised route to spike-guided deblurring that addresses practical sensor discrepancies while reconstructing a sequence, rather than just one sharpened image.
neurips-2024-spikereveal-unlocking-tempo.tldr: SpikeReveal combines blurred images with spike-camera streams in a self-supervised framework that reconstructs sharp sequences and improves reported generalization.

paragraphs: Large pretrained models can label datasets for training smaller specialist models, but repeatedly asking them for annotations can be expensive. The resulting labels also form a static dataset that can be difficult to audit. Alchemist changes what the pretrained model is asked to produce: a program that assigns labels.

Once generated, these labeling programs can be stored and run locally. They can also be reused and extended, allowing the labeling procedure itself to become a reusable artifact. This shifts the work from obtaining an individual model response for each label toward producing code that carries out the labeling process.

Across the evaluated tasks, Alchemist achieves comparable or better performance than direct language-model annotation. The authors report an average performance improvement of 12.9% and an approximately 500-fold reduction in total labeling costs across all datasets. Those figures describe the reported evaluation, rather than a fixed saving for every application. The main finding is that asking models to generate labeling programs can substantially reduce annotation costs while maintaining or improving downstream performance.
neurips-2024-the-alchemist-automated-lab.tldr: Alchemist generates reusable labeling programs, achieving comparable or better reported performance with approximately 500 times lower total labeling costs.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a transformer adapt its predictions using examples in the input without updating its parameters. Mathematical studies have investigated this behavior through linear attention, but removing softmax leaves out an important part of standard attention. This paper studies a regression formulation that retains softmax normalization.

The formulation measures the difference between a softmax prediction and a target using an L2 loss. Within this setting, the authors derive upper bounds for data transformations associated with one softmax self-attention layer and with gradient descent on the regression objective. This provides a mathematical basis for comparing attention-based transformations with changes produced through optimization.

The theoretical results indicate strong similarity between the models associated with these processes when training attention-only transformers on fundamental regression tasks. The significance is a connection between learning through contextual examples and learning through weight changes in a setting closer to standard attention than linear models. The claim remains scoped to the studied softmax-regression framework and does not assert an exact equivalence for full language models.
neurips-2024-the-closeness-of-in-context.tldr: A softmax-regression analysis establishes similarities between transformations produced by self-attention and gradient-based learning in a restricted theoretical setting.

paragraphs: Learning rates and initialization scales influence how a network’s features change, but their control is indirect. This paper introduces an angle between a layer’s feature update and its backward-pass signal as a way to describe that behavior. A feature-speed formula connects update magnitude to this angle, loss decrease, and backward-signal magnitude after a gradient-descent step.

The angle depends on the conditioning of transformations between layers. At random initialization, a kernel’s spectrum determines it; at the final layer, that kernel is the Neural Tangent Kernel. Given the angle, the formula supplies rules for selecting scales and learning rates to obtain desired feature-learning and loss-decay behavior.

The authors study ReLU multilayer perceptrons and residual networks in a limit where width grows before depth. With independent, identically distributed initialization, alignment deteriorates with depth in the multilayer perceptrons. Residual networks with branches scaled inversely with the square root of depth maintain non-degenerate alignment. These results recover properties of existing scaling rules, including μP, and motivate a new scaling for deep ReLU networks with favorable theoretical properties.
neurips-2024-the-feature-speed-formula-a.tldr: The feature-speed formula links representation updates to gradient alignment, providing principled hyperparameter-scaling rules for studied deep-network settings.

paragraphs: This paper explores converting pretrained transformers into models that use linear recurrent components such as Mamba. The aim is to retain learned capabilities while gaining favorable deployment characteristics. The conversion reuses linear projection weights from attention layers and distills the transformer with computation available through academic GPU resources.

The resulting hybrid retains one quarter of the attention layers. It achieves chat-benchmark performance comparable to the original transformer and outperforms the compared open-source hybrid Mamba models trained from scratch on trillions of tokens. The authors also introduce hardware-aware speculative decoding to accelerate generation for both Mamba and hybrid models.

Their strongest model, distilled from Llama3-8B-Instruct, scores 29.61 in length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2 against GPT-4 and 7.35 on MT-Bench. It also achieves almost perfect needle-in-a-haystack accuracy at 20 times the distillation length. These results support the feasibility of transferring an existing transformer’s capabilities into a more efficient hybrid, with the length-extrapolation evidence specifically demonstrated through the reported retrieval test.
neurips-2024-the-mamba-in-the-llama-dist.tldr: The paper distills pretrained transformers into efficient Mamba hybrids while retaining comparable chat performance and introduces faster speculative decoding.

paragraphs: Vivid-ZOO generates videos of a moving 3D object from multiple viewpoints using a text prompt. This requires the views to agree about the object while its appearance and motion remain coherent over time. Training is challenging because large captioned multi-view video collections are scarce and the model must represent both viewpoint and temporal variation.

The method separates those two dimensions so it can reuse layers from pretrained multi-view image models and conventional 2D video diffusion models. The former contribute viewpoint consistency, while the latter contribute temporal modeling. Alignment modules connect their internal representations, addressing incompatibilities caused by differences between multi-view and 2D data.

This reuse substantially reduces training cost, and the authors also contribute a captioned multi-view video dataset. Experiments across varied text prompts show videos with vivid motion, temporal coherence, and consistency across viewpoints. The paper’s main contribution is a way to combine existing spatial and temporal generation capabilities into a multi-view video system, supported by alignment between the reused model components.
neurips-2024-vivid-zoo-multi-view-video-.tldr: Vivid-ZOO combines pretrained multi-view image and video diffusion components to generate temporally coherent, consistent multi-view videos from text.
